title: Polynomial Regression & Splines
interviewAnswer: Polynomial regression adds powers or other fixed basis functions to a linear model, so it is nonlinear in x but linear in coefficients. High-degree global polynomials are often unstable and extrapolate badly. A regression spline uses low-degree polynomial pieces joined at knots, usually with continuity constraints; B-spline bases provide the same function space with better local support and conditioning. I choose knots or a smoothness penalty inside cross-validation, keep the basis transformation inside the pipeline, inspect boundary and derivative behavior, and define an explicit extrapolation policy. Coefficients depend on the basis, so I interpret the fitted curve, contrasts, or derivatives rather than raw spline coefficients.
keyPoints: Nonlinear in predictors can still be linear in fitted coefficients.
Global polynomials couple the whole domain; splines provide local flexibility.
Knots define representation, while penalties or validation control effective complexity.
Basis coefficients are coordinate-dependent; interpret functions and contrasts.
Boundary support and extrapolation policy are production requirements.
why: Many effects are smooth but not straight: demand saturates, biological response has thresholds, risk accelerates with age, and latency grows sharply near capacity. Binning loses ordering and creates discontinuities; an unconstrained high-capacity learner may obscure the shape and require much more data. Basis expansions offer a middle ground: a transparent smooth curve that fits with familiar linear-model machinery, can be regularized, and supports uncertainty calculations under declared assumptions. The representation also makes modeling choices visible. Knots express where curvature may adapt, degree expresses local shape, and boundary constraints express how the curve should behave where information is weakest. That visibility matters in production because data ranges drift and predictions outside the knot boundary can be dangerous. A spline should be chosen because it captures plausible structure and validates honestly, not because a wavy line looks impressive on training data.
intuition: A polynomial basis gives the model building blocks 1, x, x squared, x cubed, and so on. Combining them bends one curve across the entire domain. Large powers can become highly correlated, and a change needed at the right edge can disturb the left edge. A spline divides the range at knots and gives the curve extra bending freedom after each knot while constraining the pieces to meet smoothly. In a truncated cubic basis, the term (x-k)^3_+ is zero left of knot k and grows cubically to its right; adding several such terms allows changes in curvature. B-splines re-express the same piecewise-polynomial space using locally supported basis functions, so each coefficient influences only part of the range and computation is better behaved. The fitted curve is still a weighted sum of fixed columns. Complexity comes from how many basis directions are available and how strongly roughness is penalized, not from abandoning linear estimation.
deepDive: Basis expansion separates representation from estimation. Polynomials and splines both create fixed design columns, but splines localize curvature and make boundary constraints explicit. A useful model is determined by the function space, penalty, tuning design, and support policy together. Interpreting the fitted function rather than coordinate-specific basis weights keeps conclusions stable when the same curve is represented differently.
workedExample: A dose-response dataset rises quickly between doses 0 and 20, then approaches a plateau. A degree-one model misses the bend; a degree-eight global polynomial oscillates near dose 0 and rises again beyond the largest observed dose. A cubic spline with interior knots at dose quantiles captures the change in slope and a natural boundary reduces edge curvature. Validation on held-out subjects selects the basis dimension. The reported effect is the fitted contrast between doses 20 and 10 with an interval, not a raw spline coefficient.

commonMistakes.misconception: A degree-ten polynomial is simply a smoother and better version of degree two.
commonMistakes.correction: High global degree can be ill-conditioned, oscillatory, and unstable at boundaries. Complexity must be justified and validated; splines often provide safer local flexibility.

commonMistakes.misconception: Spline coefficients directly show feature importance.
commonMistakes.correction: Coefficients depend on the chosen basis and knots. Interpret the reconstructed function, contrasts, derivatives, or contribution uncertainty.

commonMistakes.misconception: More knots always create an overfit curve.
commonMistakes.correction: A rich basis plus a strong smoothness penalty can have low effective degrees of freedom. Basis dimension and effective flexibility are related but distinct.
They constrain tails to be linear beyond boundaries, which is more stable than cubic divergence but still unsupported by out-of-range data.

followUps.question: What is the difference between a regression spline and smoothing spline?
followUps.answer: A regression spline usually fixes a finite basis and estimates coefficients, optionally with a penalty. A smoothing spline uses a roughness-penalized function space whose solution has knots at observed x values but controlled effective degrees of freedom.

followUps.question: Why are B-splines numerically attractive?
followUps.answer: They have local support and better-conditioned basis behavior than raw truncated powers. Only a few basis functions are active at each x, aiding stability and sparse computation.

followUps.question: How do you model a nonlinear interaction?
followUps.answer: Use products or tensor products of basis functions, then regularize and validate them. The data must cover combinations of both predictors; otherwise the surface is weakly identified.

production: The basis transform is model state. Persist raw units, imputation, scaling, degree, knot vector, boundary knots, output-column order, coefficient vector, and extrapolation behavior. Use the same transformer object in training and serving; never recompute quantile knots from a request batch. Add golden tests at knots, boundaries, and representative interior points, plus finite-output and row-order checks. Track request share below and above training support, basis activation distributions, prediction and residual error by x range, and domain constraints such as monotonicity when required. A new data range may require collecting labels and refitting, not stretching the old curve. Compare a challenger with a simple linear baseline on a later or grouped window. Canary both transform and model, keep the previous artifact, and roll back if boundary traffic, calibration, latency, or decision-level loss exceeds declared limits.
description: Polynomial regression and splines extend linear regression to curved relationships while keeping estimation linear in coefficients. A raw high-degree polynomial is global: changing one coefficient can alter the curve everywhere, boundary behavior can become extreme, and powers can be badly conditioned. Regression splines instead join low-degree polynomial pieces at knots with continuity constraints, creating local flexibility. This chapter develops polynomial bases, truncated-power and B-spline representations, knot placement, natural boundary constraints, smoothing penalties, effective degrees of freedom, and honest complexity selection. You will distinguish interpolation from regression smoothing and understand why basis coefficients are usually less meaningful than the fitted function and its derivatives. A worked dose-response example shows how a cubic spline captures a plateau without forcing oscillation across the domain. The lab builds a truncated cubic regression-spline basis, uses scikit-learn's local B-spline transformer, and verifies continuity, rank, held-out error, and row-order invariance. Production guidance treats knots, boundaries, scaling, and extrapolation policy as versioned model state. Splines improve a conditional-mean specification over observed support; they do not solve confounding, sparse boundary data, or unsupported extrapolation.
learningObjectives: Explain why polynomial and spline regression remain linear in parameters while modeling nonlinear functions.
Construct a regression-spline basis and relate knots, degree, continuity, and effective flexibility.
Choose complexity using leakage-safe validation and diagnose unstable boundary or extrapolation behavior.
Deploy a basis transform with reproducible knots, scaling, and out-of-range behavior.

deepSections.title: Global polynomial regression and its limits
deepSections.body: A degree-m polynomial regression specifies f(x)=beta0+beta1 x+...+beta_m x^m. With columns [1,x,...,x^m], least squares or a generalized-linear-model likelihood estimates beta. The model is linear in beta, so projection and regularization tools still apply. Raw powers can be severely ill-conditioned when x has a large range or m is high. Centering and scaling x, or using orthogonal polynomial bases, improves numerical behavior without changing the function space over the training domain. Degree is a model-selection choice and must be evaluated out of sample. High degree does not guarantee useful local flexibility: polynomial behavior is global and can oscillate between observations, especially near boundaries. Extrapolation is dictated by the highest-degree term and can explode. A polynomial may be appropriate when physics supplies a low-degree approximation over a narrow range, but it is rarely wise to increase degree until a training curve passes through every point. Interpolation answers a different question from estimating a noisy conditional mean. The uncertainty in a fitted curve includes coefficient estimation and, for a new observation, outcome noise; it does not cover arbitrary model misspecification.

deepSections.title: Piecewise polynomials joined at knots
deepSections.body: Choose interior knots k1,...,kK. A degree-one piecewise model can have different slopes by interval; imposing continuity removes jumps. A cubic regression spline is piecewise cubic and conventionally continuous through its first and second derivatives at each knot. One representation uses [1,x,x^2,x^3,(x-k1)^3_+,...,(x-kK)^3_+]. Continuity is built into this truncated-power basis. Its columns can still be correlated, so B-splines are preferred computationally. A B-spline basis has local support: only a small number of basis functions are nonzero at any x. Knots can be placed at predictor quantiles to allocate flexibility where data are dense, or at scientifically meaningful thresholds. More knots increase the available function space but do not alone determine effective wiggliness when coefficients are penalized. Natural cubic splines impose linear behavior beyond boundary knots, reducing unstable edge curvature, though linear extrapolation can still be wrong. Restricted cubic splines use related constraints. Store the learned knot sequence and boundary knots; recomputing quantiles independently during serving changes the model.

deepSections.title: Select complexity without looking at the answer
deepSections.body: Regression splines choose a modest basis dimension and fit coefficients; smoothing splines conceptually allow knots at each distinct x but penalize integrated squared second derivative, balancing residual fit with roughness. Penalized B-splines combine a rich B-spline basis with difference or derivative penalties. The tuning parameter controls effective degrees of freedom continuously: zero penalty approaches a flexible fit; a strong second-derivative penalty approaches a straight line. Select degree, knot count, and penalty using cross-validation that respects time or groups. Do not choose knots after inspecting test residuals. Uncertainty bands conditional on chosen tuning can understate model-selection uncertainty; bootstrap the whole tuning pipeline when that uncertainty matters. Simultaneous bands differ from pointwise intervals because they cover a whole function. Inspect derivative estimates only where data support them, since differentiation amplifies noise. For interpretability, report predicted contrasts such as f(30)-f(20), slopes over declared intervals, and uncertainty. Raw basis coefficients depend on knot placement and basis rotation and rarely have standalone meaning.

deepSections.title: Boundaries, interactions, and serving behavior
deepSections.body: Curves are least constrained near and beyond the observed boundaries. Plot the data density under the fitted function and report training support. Define whether out-of-range x is rejected, clipped, linearly extrapolated under a natural spline, or routed to another model. Clipping can create plateaus and hide genuine changes, so it is a policy rather than a neutral fix. With multiple predictors, apply separate spline bases for additive effects or tensor-product bases for interactions. A full tensor grows quickly and needs structured regularization. If the effect of dose differs by population, an interaction between a spline basis and group indicator lets the entire curve vary by group; enough data in each region are required. Missing-value handling, scaling, knot selection, and category encoding must be inside the pipeline. Monitor input support, basis activation, boundary traffic, residuals by range, and derivative or monotonicity constraints important to the domain. A visually smooth curve can still be causally biased or operationally unsafe if features are measured after the outcome or the deployed range shifts.

math: A truncated cubic regression spline with knots k_j is f(x)=beta0+beta1 x+beta2 x^2+beta3 x^3+sum_j gamma_j(x-k_j)_+^3, where (u)_+=max(u,0). This form has continuous first and second derivatives at every knot. A smoothing formulation minimizes sum_i[y_i-f(x_i)]^2 + lambda integral [f''(t)]^2 dt. Lambda=0 favors fit; lambda approaching infinity suppresses curvature toward a line. A B-spline basis writes f(x)=sum_m theta_m B_m(x), usually with sparse local basis support and a coefficient roughness penalty.

workedExamples.title: Construct a one-knot cubic basis
workedExamples.body: For knot k=2, rows use [1,x,x^2,x^3,(x-2)^3_+]. At x=1 the last term is zero; at x=3 it is one; at x=4 it is eight. The new coefficient changes curvature only to the right of two. Because the added term and its first two derivatives equal zero at the knot, the joined curve is twice continuously differentiable.

workedExamples.title: A contrast is more interpretable than a basis weight
workedExamples.body: Suppose five B-spline coefficients have no obvious unit interpretation. Evaluate the same stored basis at x=20 and x=10, subtract the two basis rows, and multiply by theta. That yields f(20)-f(10) in outcome units. Its covariance follows from the same contrast vector and coefficient covariance, conditional on tuning.

lab.goal: Build a truncated cubic regression spline, use a local B-spline pipeline, and verify continuity, rank, row-order invariance, and nonlinear held-out improvement.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def truncated_cubic(x,knots):
    x=np.asarray(x,float).reshape(-1)
    cols=[np.ones_like(x),x,x**2,x**3]
    cols += [np.maximum(x-k,0.0)**3 for k in knots]
    return np.column_stack(cols)
def fit_spline(x,y,knots,ridge=1e-8):
    B=truncated_cubic(x,knots); P=np.eye(B.shape[1]); P[0,0]=0
    coef=np.linalg.solve(B.T@B+ridge*P,B.T@np.asarray(y,float))
    return coef
rng=np.random.default_rng(4)
x=np.linspace(0,1,100); y=np.sin(2.5*np.pi*x)+rng.normal(0,.08,len(x))
train=np.arange(len(x))%5!=0; test=~train; knots=[.25,.5,.75]
coef=fit_spline(x[train],y[train],knots)
pred=truncated_cubic(x[test],knots)@coef
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge,LinearRegression
model=make_pipeline(SplineTransformer(n_knots=5,degree=3,include_bias=False),Ridge(alpha=1e-3)).fit(x[train,None],y[train])
sk_pred=model.predict(x[test,None])
linear=LinearRegression().fit(x[train,None],y[train])
lab.verifyIt:
assert truncated_cubic(x,knots).shape==(100,7)
assert np.linalg.matrix_rank(truncated_cubic(x[train],knots))==7
for k in knots:
    eps=1e-6
    left=truncated_cubic([k-eps],knots)@coef
    right=truncated_cubic([k+eps],knots)@coef
    assert abs((left-right).item())<1e-4
linear_mse=np.mean((linear.predict(x[test,None])-y[test])**2)
spline_mse=np.mean((sk_pred-y[test])**2)
assert spline_mse<0.45*linear_mse
perm=np.random.default_rng(9).permutation(train.sum())
coef_perm=fit_spline(x[train][perm],y[train][perm],knots)
assert np.allclose(coef_perm,coef,atol=1e-6)
assert np.isfinite(pred).all()
lab.shipIt: Persist scaling, degree, knots, boundaries, coefficient and extrapolation policy in one artifact; test golden basis rows and boundary inputs, monitor support and boundary traffic, and roll back the full transform-plus-model pipeline when range or error criteria fail.

exercises.prompt: Why is y=beta0+beta1 x+beta2 x^2 still a linear regression model?
exercises.solution: The function is nonlinear in x but linear in unknown coefficients beta. Once x and x squared are design columns, ordinary linear estimation applies.

exercises.prompt: A fitted spline behaves wildly just beyond the largest training x. Give two remedies.
exercises.solution: Use defensible boundary constraints such as a natural spline and define reject, route, or limited extrapolation policy. More importantly, collect data in the needed region rather than presenting unsupported tails as evidence.

exercises.prompt: How would you compare two basis representations that span the same function space?
exercises.solution: Compare fitted values, predictions, contrasts, derivatives, and numerical conditioning. Raw coefficients can differ because they are coordinates in different bases.
